turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, give me a sec, this login's spinning again. Err. Right. What brings you in?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, nah, it's nothing. He booked it, not me.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's not nothing. She's crying all the time and she doesn't sleep, even when the bub's asleep. I'm worried.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hang on, the screen just jumped. Say that again? What's the actual problem?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm not sleeping. That's why he dragged me. It's not a big deal.
[SEG0006] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Bub is six weeks old. She just lies there awake.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): The not sleeping, I was gonna say six weeks, no, more like four. He sleeps, I don't.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): Four weeks, awake even when he sleeps. Mm. And mood?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): I get a bit teary. Mostly in the evenings, last few weeks. Everyone does after a baby.
[SEG0010] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She was sobbing into the washing this morning. She keeps saying she's fine.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, can you hold on, I'm clicking the wrong tab. Any thoughts of hurting yourself, or the baby?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Never. I wouldn't do that.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good, thank you. Umm, file says asthma. Is that still a thing?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, since I was a kid. Hardly bothers me.
[SEG0015] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She keeps the blue puffer in the nappy bag.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): What are you actually using? Slow down, I've lost the medication list.
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Ventalin... umm, ventolin. Two puffs, four times a day... no, not four times, only when I need it, couple of times a week.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ventolin when you need it. Any tablets?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Just the iron. Ferrograd. Seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty milligrams, once a day. Midwife put me on it.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): 150, once a day. Any reactions to medicines? Rashes, swelling?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Penicillan. That's a proper allergy. Hives all over, and my lips blew up.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Penicillin, hives and swollen lips. We won't touch that family. When did it happen?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Uh, no idea. Last winter, or the one before. Maybe uni. I can't date it.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Date's a blur, allergy still stands. Back to the asthma, sorry, this alert keeps popping. Any wheeze?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): No... well, sometimes. At night. Not that I care.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sometimes at night. Shortness of breath?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Not that either. I'm not puffed.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Chest pain?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Never.
[SEG0030] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): See, chest is fine. It's the coping. I offer to do the night feeds and she won't hand him over.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): I can manage. It's tiredness. I'm not, like, depressed.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm not putting a label on it today. Could be baby blues dragging on, or early postnatal depression. I honestly can't tell yet.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): So it's nothing. Can we wrap up? Computer's annoying you anyway.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): It's not nothing. I want you back in a fortnight, book it, not an if. And I'll refer you to the child health nurse for some extra support this week.
[SEG0035] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll get her here. I'll do the nights if she lets me. We've been going in circles about it.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let him take some nights, please. If any thoughts of hurting yourself or the bub show up, ring us or go to emergency the same day. And no penicillin, obviously.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, fine. Pram's in a loading zone, so. We're good.

spec.situation: Mother six weeks after delivery, tearful, not sleeping even when the baby sleeps; partner present and anxious; denies harming herself or the baby when asked directly; support and follow-up planned.

traps.happens: The patient denies some symptoms (said as 'no', 'not really', 'never'), has a chronic condition named earlier (for example asthma or hypertension) and later the doctor asks about another symptom of it, and one answer is a double negative or a correction ('not that either', 'no... well, sometimes').
traps.label_rule: Denials go in negative_findings with the exact thing denied, never in symptoms. NEVER write a negative about a condition the patient has said they have. A corrected answer keeps only the final version. A negative is never a symptom, and 'not painful' is the finding 'pain' absent, not a symptom called 'painless'.

traps.happens: The doctor asks about drug reactions. Variants (use ONE per encounter): (a) the patient says 'No, never, I have taken penicillin and everything' (no allergy); (b) the patient is unsure ('maybe the antibiotic or the painkiller, nobody told me which'); (c) a real allergy with the reaction described; (d) allergies are never asked.
traps.label_rule: (a) NO allergy entry: negative_findings 'Allergies' absent. (b) allergy with status uncertain, the substance as described, the reaction if said, plus an allergy_uncertain uncertainty. (c) allergy with the reaction. (d) nothing at all. NEVER list a medicine the patient has taken without a reaction as an allergy, and the plan must not prescribe a drug of a recorded allergy's family.

features: self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.
vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats

omissions.text: Patient denied being short of breath, saying 'I'm not puffed.'
Patient said she is not 'like, depressed,' indicating she does not identify with depression despite the doctor's differential.
